description: AI Science Club from University of Gdańsk, Poland
summary:
Choosing your next crop takes more than checking the weather. CropTips brings your soil, past crops, water and equipment together to help you decide what could grow next. Choose what matters to you: a good harvest, healthier soil, less water or earning more, in a simple, easy-to-use dashboard.

This is a demo for California only. It supports planting now; planning for later dates and multiple years is not available yet. Select "California demo" in the app to explore Valley Farm: a 32-hectare example farm in Fresno County with three sectors.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

CropTips helps US farmers decide what to plant next. The farmer describes their field: location, soil texture, pH, land capability class, irrigation, nearest river station, past crops, equipment and what they care about most (soil health, harvest, water, profit). CropTips then ranks crops from the FAO EcoCrop database. It checks each crop against the soil and pH, warns when a related crop family was grown there recently, and weights the result by the farmer’s goals.

Next to the ranking, the app shows a 100-day regional outlook for air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture and soil temperature. We built it from NASA data: SMAP for soil, MERRA-2 for air temperature and wind, and GPM IMERG for rain. Gradient boosting models predict a central estimate plus an 80% uncertainty range for ten 10-day windows and for the whole period.

The app also has live water and fire alerts (USGS, NWS, NIFC), PRISM climate maps, short growing tips with a quiz, and an equipment tracker. Tip, a mascot chatbot, answers questions using a small AI model that runs locally. It only draws on reviewed sources such as UC Cooperative Extension and EcoCrop.

What benefits does it have?

  • Small and mid-size farmers get one place to see soil fit, crop rotation, regional conditions and hazards, instead of piecing it together from many sites.
  • Every recommendation comes with reasons and warnings in plain language.
  • Using NASA satellite and reanalysis data gives regional conditions where a farmer has no sensors.
  • It works on a laptop with no paid AI service, so it could be run cheaply by a co-op or extension office.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We wanted to show that open NASA Earth data can be turned into advice a non-expert can use. CropTips is a decision aid, not a guarantee, and it says so on every screen.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: JavaScript with React 19, Vite, React Router, Leaflet.
  • Backend: Python with Django 5.2 and SQLite.
  • Data and ML: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (HistGradientBoostingRegressor), xarray, netCDF4, shapely, pyproj, joblib.
  • Data sources: NASA SMAP, MERRA-2 and GPM IMERG through NASA Earthdata. Also USGS, NWS, NIFC, PRISM, FAO EcoCrop and UC Extension guides.
  • AI assistant: retrieval over SQLite FTS5 plus embeddings, using Ollama with ministral-3:3b and embeddinggemma.
  • Other: LaTeX for the API docs, Git for version control.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. Everything runs locally, with the assistant on CPU.

How is your project creative?

  • We combined three different NASA products into one outlook that is easy to read, with the uncertainty shown, not hidden.
  • Crop ranking responds to what each farmer wants, not just to the soil.
  • We report the limits honestly. The charts show how often the shaded range really contained the true value in tests, and the app states that it uses NASA model values, not field sensors.
  • The AI assistant is private and cheap to run: it works offline and is limited to reviewed sources.
  • The overall site is friendly, so it feels approachable for people who don’t use data tools.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: the soil moisture model clearly beats a simple seasonal average at 1 to 10 days. For air temperature it mostly ties the baseline, and the intervals covered about 75% of cases against the 80% target. We show this in the app.
  • Time and place: we split train, validation and test data by date, and held out 25% of locations, to avoid leaking future data into training.
  • Data limits: the record is only about five years (November 2021 to October 2026). Soil temperature is a research product from one daily 13:30 UTC sample, and the 100-day outlook uses no weather forecast.
  • Safety: the app flags weak data, avoids implying that regional estimates are field measurements, and repeats that it’s a guide, not a guarantee.
  • Privacy and cost: The chat sends no history or profile to any cloud service.
  • Scope: We focused on a single state, in this case California, so that crop, water and hazard data could be checked properly.
